_style: Address the user with informal singular “ti” (dy, dy hun, -a imperatives: “Gwiria”, “Ysgrifenna”), never “chi” for one person; for the couple together use plural “chi” / “chi'ch dau” / “eich” (“eich taith”, “gyda'ch gilydd”). The other person is always “dy bartner” (partner, soft-mutated after dy) or their name; avoid the pronouns “e/fe/fo” and “hi” for the partner and rephrase with “dy bartner” or the name, and avoid gendered words such as cariad-bachgen/cariad-merch, gŵr, gwraig. Apply normal Welsh mutations to ordinary words, but a placeholder (%@, %1$@, numbers) is never mutated or declined and must not follow a word that would require mutating it or choosing a/ac, ei/ei (his/her): rephrase instead (e.g. “Neges gan %@” is fine; avoid “a %@”, write “%@ a ti” as “chi'ch dau”). Quote marks: single curly ‘ ’ outside, double “ ” inside; apostrophe ’ in contractions may stay straight ' as in the source (i'r, gyda'ch); ellipsis “…” as one character; no space before ? ! : ; and keep “ · ”, emoji, \n and Coupley unchanged; keep circumflex and other diacritics (ŵ, ŷ, â, ô, ê) correct, Latin script only. Numbers: decimal point “.”, thousands separator “,”; dates day–month–year (“14 Tachwedd 2026”), 24-hour time; numerals with a noun take the singular noun (“%lld diwrnod”, “%lld atgof”), and with digits do not mutate the noun. Plural categories for Welsh are zero, one, two, few, many, other: fill all six (with digits normally the same singular-noun text in each, e.g. zero “%lld diwrnod”, one “%lld diwrnod”, two “%lld diwrnod”, few “%lld diwrnod”, many “%lld diwrnod”, other “%lld diwrnod”; spelled-out forms may use correct mutations like “dau ddiwrnod”). Buttons and actions are short verb-nouns (“Cadw”, “Anfon llythyr”, “Ceisio eto”, “Plannu”, “Dyfrio”); titles, tabs, chips and buttons use sentence case (capital on first word only, except proper names, Coupley, Premium, AI). Tone: warm, light, natural modern Welsh (as spoken, not formal or legalistic), never cheesy; prefer common words over coinages and English loanwords where Welsh speakers already use them (cwis, coffi, teclyn).
